entries.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis included 38 randomized controlled trials with 2,709 participants receiving elemental magnesium for at least 4 weeks; doses ranged from 82.3 to 637 mg/day and study heterogeneity was high.
Across the 38 randomized trials, magnesium supplementation reduced systolic blood pressure by a pooled mean difference of 2.81 mm Hg versus placebo (95% CI 1.29 to 4.32 mm Hg lower).
The same meta-analysis found a pooled diastolic blood-pressure reduction of 2.05 mm Hg versus placebo (95% CI 0.88 to 3.23 mm Hg lower).

Larger pooled blood-pressure reductions were observed among hypertensive participants already receiving blood-pressure medication and among participants with hypomagnesemia; these subgroup effects should not be generalized to normotensive or magnesium-replete adults.

The magnesium blood-pressure meta-analysis did not reach statistical significance in normotensive groups and found no clear dose-response relationship; high between-study heterogeneity limits claims of a universal or optimal dose.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized controlled trials involving 444 people with metabolic syndrome evaluated oral magnesium supplementation for at least two months against placebo on inflammatory markers.
In participants with metabolic syndrome, long-term oral magnesium supplementation reduced serum C-reactive protein with a pooled standardized mean difference of -0.327 (95% CI -0.602 to -0.053).

CRP subgroup signals were more apparent in 12- and 16-week studies, women, and tablet or capsule interventions, while other subgroup estimates became non-significant; these findings remain population- and formulation-specific rather than a general anti-inflammatory claim.

A 2025 systematic review identified 13 randomized controlled trials of green tea, green tea extract, matcha, EGCG, or L-theanine for mood-related symptoms, with substantial intervention and outcome heterogeneity.
Within the 13-trial green-tea review, four studies reported improvements in depressive symptoms; the review did not establish that all green-tea preparations have equivalent antidepressant effects.

The green-tea review reported improvements in anxiety symptoms in six studies, stress symptoms in five, and sleep symptoms in one, but the interventions ranged across whole tea, extracts, matcha, EGCG, and L-theanine and should not be collapsed into one interchangeable treatment.

No included randomized trial in the 2025 review found a statistically significant effect of green tea or its studied bioactive compounds on brain-derived neurotrophic factor, providing a mechanistic null boundary against inferring BDNF-mediated clinical benefit.

A systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized 26 randomized controlled trials involving 1,755 adults with overweight or obesity and characterized the pooled cardiometabolic effects of probiotic supplementation as small and not yet conclusive.

In adults with overweight or obesity, the pooled probiotic estimate for systolic blood pressure was not statistically significant, while the pooled diastolic blood-pressure effect was small; this does not support a broad antihypertensive claim.

The overweight/obesity probiotic meta-analysis reported small pooled changes in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides, while HDL cholesterol did not show a significant pooled change; strain and formulation differences remain important.

The same meta-analysis reported a small pooled reduction in C-reactive protein (SMD -0.34; 95% CI -0.63 to -0.05) in adults with overweight or obesity, which should remain a biomarker finding rather than a disease-treatment claim.

A published correction applies to the 2025 probiotic cardiometabolic meta-analysis (original DOI 10.1002/fsn3.70434); downstream evidence extraction should use the corrected article and avoid propagating unverified original numeric fields.

A systematic review included 23 randomized controlled trials with 1,401 clinically diagnosed participants, with 20 trials contributing to meta-analysis of probiotic, prebiotic, or synbiotic interventions for depression or anxiety symptoms.

Across clinical samples, probiotic interventions were associated with lower depression symptom scores (pooled SMD -0.96; 95% CI -1.31 to -0.61), but high heterogeneity limits assumptions of a uniform effect across products or populations.

Probiotic interventions in clinically diagnosed samples were associated with a moderate pooled reduction in anxiety symptoms (SMD -0.59; 95% CI -0.98 to -0.19), with formulation and trial-duration differences contributing to heterogeneity.

In the same review, prebiotic interventions did not produce a statistically significant pooled reduction in depression symptoms (SMD -0.28; 95% CI -0.61 to 0.04), separating prebiotic evidence from the probiotic signal.

The clinical depression/anxiety meta-analysis reported high heterogeneity and identified study duration and probiotic formulation as contributors, so evidence should remain strain-, formulation-, population-, and outcome-specific rather than a class-wide mental-health claim.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomized studies involving 3,350 healthy working adults found a modest pooled improvement across subclinical depression, anxiety, and stress outcomes with probiotics (SMD -0.21; 95% CI -0.34 to -0.09).

In healthy working adults, probiotic interventions were associated with lower cortisol (SMD -0.26; 95% CI -0.45 to -0.08), while C-reactive protein did not show a statistically significant pooled effect.

The working-adult probiotic review found moderate heterogeneity related to strains, doses, and intervention duration, and available evidence was insufficient for firm conclusions on sleep quality or oxidative-stress biomarkers; findings remain preliminary.
